mouth.title: An oral biofilm
mouth.description: Sugars enter the plaque; neighbouring organisms exchange the acids they produce.

zones.name: Food & sugars
zones.text: Sugar becomes fuel for streptococci, which release lactate into the biofilm.

zones.name: Saliva
zones.text: Saliva moves food and microbes between oral surfaces.

zones.name: Biofilm
zones.text: Veillonella consumes lactate from neighbouring fermenters. Microscopy reveals organised communities around these exchanges.

oesophagus.title: A living passage
oesophagus.description: Swallowed organisms meet a surface shaped by movement, mucus, and reflux.

zones.name: Passing contents
zones.text: Swallowing continually delivers oral bacteria and food.

zones.name: Moving fluid
zones.text: Coordinated muscular movement carries this material toward the stomach.

zones.name: At the surface
zones.text: Biopsies recovered Streptococcus and Veillonella from distal oesophageal tissue.

stomach.title: Life at an acid boundary
stomach.description: Meals, acid and mucus create several habitats inside one chamber. The contents are mixed and emptied, while the wall maintains a protective boundary.

zones.name: Food arrivals
zones.text: Meals and swallowed saliva introduce microbes alongside nutrients. Food temporarily changes acidity, and survival through this chamber affects which organisms reach the intestine.

zones.name: Acidic contents
zones.text: Acid and digestive enzymes act on the moving contents. Changing acid production changes this ecological filter, with effects that can extend into the intestinal community.

zones.name: Mucus & lining
zones.text: Mucus and bicarbonate protect the stomach wall from its own acid. This creates a gradient between the contents and the cells, giving surface-associated organisms a different environment. H. pylori is one well-studied specialist of this niche.

small.title: A moving food landscape
small.description: Microbes intercept sugars while the host absorbs nutrients. Bile and movement continually reshape the habitat.

zones.name: Meal-derived sugars
zones.text: Small-intestinal Streptococcus actively expresses systems for taking up and processing carbohydrates.

zones.name: Flowing contents
zones.text: Veillonella consumes lactate produced by neighbouring fermenters.

zones.name: At the lining
zones.text: Introduced probiotic organisms settle unevenly across people and intestinal sites.

colon.title: A landscape of exchange
colon.description: Food particles, flowing contents, and mucus each offer different resources and neighbours.

zones.name: On food particles
zones.text: Bacteroides breaks down complex sugars. Bifidobacteria produce acetate and lactate that feed other organisms.

zones.name: In the contents
zones.text: Fermentation products move between cells. Methanobrevibacter consumes hydrogen and formate; phages follow their bacterial hosts.

zones.name: Mucus & lining
zones.text: Akkermansia uses mucin. Fungi and bacterial products interact with the barrier and its immune cells.

rectum.title: The downstream community
rectum.description: Stool carries cells and fermentation products from colonic communities into the final passage.

zones.name: Remaining material
zones.text: Remaining substrates and microbial cells arrive after fermentation upstream.

zones.name: Cells & gases
zones.text: Transit changes how long substrates remain available. Breath methane is associated with constipation.

zones.name: The final surface
zones.text: A stool sample is a downstream collection of a spatially varied gut ecosystem.

stories.title: Sugar, acid & teeth
stories.subtitle: Repeated sugar exposure changes plaque chemistry and the minerals in enamel.
stories.evidence: Laboratory biofilms · human intra-oral enamel experiments

steps.label: Dietary sugars
steps.detail: Sugar reaching plaque supplies fermentable carbohydrate. Sucrose also supports the sticky material that holds biofilms together.

steps.label: Streptococcus
steps.detail: S. mutans ferments sugar in the experimental biofilm. Frequent sucrose exposures change its acid-producing behaviour.

steps.label: Organic acids
steps.detail: Bacterial fermentation releases acids, including lactate. With repeated sugar exposure, the biofilm spends more time in acidic conditions.

steps.label: Plaque acidity
steps.detail: The acidic environment reaches the enamel below the biofilm. Saliva flow, the meal pattern and the surrounding community influence this environment.

steps.label: Enamel minerals
steps.detail: The studies measured enamel demineralisation alongside changes in plaque. This connects microbial sugar use to the process leading to dental decay.

stories.title: One microbe feeds another
stories.subtitle: Lactate connects sugar-fermenting bacteria with neighbours in the same biofilm.
stories.evidence: Saliva-fed flow-cell biofilms · defined bacterial communities

steps.label: Salivary nutrients
steps.detail: Researchers supplied saliva to small, defined bacterial communities on a surface.

steps.label: Streptococcus
steps.detail: S. oralis produced lactate while growing on nutrients in saliva.

steps.label: Lactate
steps.detail: The fermentation product becomes a food source for another organism in the same neighbourhood.

steps.label: Veillonella
steps.detail: Veillonella consumed lactate and supported growth in paired communities.

steps.label: A growing biofilm
steps.detail: The partnership helped mixed communities develop. Imaging of human plaque reveals the spatial neighbourhoods in which such exchanges take place.

stories.title: From tongue to stomach
stories.subtitle: Oral microbes start a chemical journey that crosses the oesophagus.
stories.evidence: Human tongue isolates · dietary nitrate experiments · junction microsensors

steps.label: Salivary nitrate
steps.detail: After a dietary nitrate load, nitrate becomes concentrated in saliva and reaches bacteria on the tongue.

steps.label: Tongue bacteria
steps.detail: Veillonella, Rothia and Actinomyces isolates reduce nitrate to nitrite. Activity is concentrated at the rear of the tongue.

steps.label: Swallowed nitrite
steps.detail: Swallowed saliva carries nitrite down the oesophagus. The microbial conversion happened upstream, on the tongue.

steps.label: The acid boundary
steps.detail: At the oesophagus–stomach junction, nitrite meets acidic gastric juice. Microsensors locate the peak of nitric oxide formation at this boundary.

steps.label: Nitric oxide
steps.detail: Acid chemistry produces nitric oxide from nitrite. A human nitrate experiment measured a large, sustained rise in gastric nitric oxide.

stories.title: Fibre becomes butyrate
stories.subtitle: A meal passes through a microbial partnership.
stories.evidence: Bacterial cocultures · fermentation enzymes · mouse colonocytes

steps.label: Food carbohydrates
steps.detail: Starch or fructooligosaccharides supply fermentable carbohydrate.

steps.label: Bifidobacterium
steps.detail: B. adolescentis breaks down the substrate and releases acetate.

steps.label: Acetate
steps.detail: Acetate passes into a shared pool available to neighbouring bacteria.

steps.label: Faecalibacterium
steps.detail: F. prausnitzii uses acetate during fermentation. Cocultures produced more butyrate than its monocultures.

steps.label: Butyrate
steps.detail: Carbon exchanged between organisms becomes another fermentation product: butyrate.

steps.label: The gut lining
steps.detail: In mouse colonocytes, bacterial butyrate fuels mitochondrial respiration. Adding it restored energy metabolism in cells from germ-free animals.

stories.title: Hydrogen becomes methane
stories.subtitle: A bacterial fermentation supports an archaeal neighbour.

steps.label: Food substrates
steps.detail: Bacteroides ferments dietary carbohydrates.

steps.label: Bacteroides
steps.detail: Fermentation releases products that support Methanobrevibacter growth.

steps.label: Hydrogen & formate
steps.detail: These fermentation products become fuel for methanogens.

steps.label: Methanobrevibacter
steps.detail: The archaeon consumes bacterial products and releases methane.

steps.label: Methane & transit
steps.detail: Human studies associate breath methane with constipation and slower transit.

stories.title: Muscle, lactate, microbes
stories.subtitle: An exchange connecting exercise with the gut.

steps.label: Exercising muscle
steps.detail: Exercise produces lactate. Veillonella abundance rose after a marathon in the human observations.

steps.label: Blood lactate
steps.detail: Tracer experiments in mice followed lactate from blood into the intestinal lumen.

steps.label: Veillonella
steps.detail: An isolate from a runner consumed lactate.

steps.label: Propionate
steps.detail: Veillonella converted lactate into propionate.

steps.label: Endurance in mice
steps.detail: The isolate increased mouse treadmill endurance; propionate reproduced the effect in the experiment.

stories.title: Urea and a local refuge
stories.subtitle: How H. pylori lives beside the stomach lining.
stories.evidence: Mucin experiments · channel genetics · human eradication trial

steps.label: Gastric mucus
steps.detail: In a gastric mucin model, H. pylori changes the gel around it and gains room to swim.

steps.label: Helicobacter pylori
steps.detail: H. pylori makes urease. Its acid-sensitive UreI channel opens a route for urea to enter the cell.

steps.label: Urea breakdown
steps.detail: Inside the cell, urease breaks urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Deletion experiments connect urea entry to enzyme activation in acid.

steps.label: Local buffering
steps.detail: The products of urea breakdown buffer acidity. In the mucin model, the pH shift also loosens the gel around the bacterium.

steps.label: Persistent infection
steps.detail: Long-term infection can drive gastritis. Eradication reduced gastric cancer incidence in a long-followed human trial.

stories.title: A food molecule becomes a signal
stories.subtitle: L. reuteri links histidine to immune-cell signalling.

steps.label: Histidine
steps.detail: The amino acid supplies the starting material.

steps.label: Lactobacillus reuteri
steps.detail: L. reuteri 6475 carries a histidine-decarboxylase pathway.

steps.label: Histamine
steps.detail: The pathway converts histidine into histamine.

steps.label: H₂ receptor
steps.detail: Bacterial histamine activates H₂ receptors in human immune-cell experiments.

steps.label: TNF production falls
steps.detail: Intracellular signalling changes and inflammatory TNF production decreases.

connections.title: The intestinal barrier
connections.route: Bifidobacterium → acetate → intestinal cells → reduced toxin passage
connections.description: In an E. coli infection model, acetate-producing bifidobacteria reduced the movement of Shiga toxin from the gut into blood.

connections.title: Immune development
connections.route: B. fragilis → polysaccharide A → immune cells → T-cell development
connections.description: A defined bacterial surface molecule changed immune development. Bacteria lacking polysaccharide A did not restore the same functions.

connections.title: Metabolic health
connections.route: A. muciniphila preparation → measured metabolic outcomes
connections.description: Pasteurised A. muciniphila improved insulin sensitivity and some other metabolic measures in a small human trial. The complete route from preparation to outcome remains an experimental question.

connections.title: Muscle and performance
connections.route: Exercising muscle → blood lactate → gut Veillonella → propionate
connections.description: Lactate made during exercise became fuel for a gut organism. Mouse experiments linked the isolate and its fermentation product with increased endurance.

connections.title: Brain and behaviour
connections.signal: Nerves, precursors, immune and metabolic signals
connections.evidence: Neural, metabolic and immune experiments + human studies
connections.route: Gut sensing and microbial metabolism ↔ neural, immune and hormonal communication ↔ brain
connections.description: The gut and brain exchange signals through sensory nerves, tryptophan metabolism, immune responses and microbial products. Serotonin helps turn local gut sensing into neural activity. The connected maps follow each route and the experiments behind it.
